How Google Ads Works: Intent, the Auction and the Numbers

Before you touch a client's money, you need to understand what Google is actually selling: a place in front of a person at the moment they search, scroll or watch. This module explains the ad auction and Quality Score, the main campaign types and when each fits, and the business arithmetic that tells you how much a click is worth.

Most advertising interrupts people. A billboard on the Third Mainland Bridge or a sponsored post on Instagram reaches people who were doing something else. A **search ad** is different: it appears only after a person has typed what they want into Google. When someone in Ibadan types "inverter installation near me", they are telling you their need, their location and often their urgency. This is called **search intent**, and it is the main reason Google Ads can turn money into leads faster than most other channels.
A person using a search engine on a large screen
A search ad answers a question the customer has already asked, which is why intent comes first in this course.
What happens in the half second after a search

Every time a search happens, Google runs an **auction** among all advertisers whose keywords match that search. The auction decides whether any ad shows, which ads show, in what order, and how much each advertiser pays if their ad is clicked. Nobody books a fixed spot. The auction runs again for the very next search, so your position can change from one search to the next.
Google calls the score that sets your position **Ad Rank**. According to Google Ads Help, Ad Rank is calculated from six things:
**Your bid**: the most you are willing to pay for one click.
**Ad and landing page quality**: how relevant and useful your ad and the page behind it are to this search.
**Ad Rank thresholds**: minimum standards an ad must reach to show at all, or to show above the organic results.
**Competitiveness of the auction**: if two ads have very similar Ad Rank, each has a similar chance of the higher spot.
**Context of the search**: the words used, the person's location, device, time of day and other signals.
**Expected impact of assets**: how much extra information such as a phone number or sitelinks is likely to help.

Worked example: why the biggest bid can lose

For example, three installers in Ibadan bid on the same search. To see the logic, we use the classic textbook model (Ad Rank = bid x quality, on a 1 to 10 scale). Google's real auction uses more factors, but the lesson is the same. Naira figures are illustrative.
Installer A bids ₦300 with quality 8. Ad Rank = 300 x 8 = 2,400.
Installer B bids ₦500 with quality 4. Ad Rank = 500 x 4 = 2,000.
Installer C bids ₦250 with quality 6. Ad Rank = 250 x 6 = 1,500.
Order on the page: A first, B second, C third, even though B bid the most.
In the textbook model, each advertiser pays just enough to beat the Ad Rank below them. A pays 2,000 / 8 = ₦250, plus a token ₦1, so about ₦251. B pays 1,500 / 4 = ₦375, plus ₦1, so about ₦376.
Installer A holds the top spot and pays about ₦251 per click, while Installer B sits lower and pays about ₦376. Better relevance bought a higher position for less money.

Notice two things. First, your **maximum CPC** (cost per click) is a ceiling, not the price. The **actual CPC** is usually lower. Second, quality is a lever you control. Improving relevance and landing pages is often cheaper than raising bids.

Search ads can show above or below the organic (unpaid) results and carry a "Sponsored" label. They can also run on Google Search Partners, other sites that use Google search, unless you switch that off in the campaign settings. Organic ranking comes from SEO and you cannot buy it; paid placement comes from the auction. A business can have both, and many do.

YouTube ad formats in brief

**Skippable in-stream**: plays before, during or after a video; the viewer can skip after 5 seconds. With cost-per-view bidding you generally pay when someone watches 30 seconds (or the whole ad if shorter) or interacts.
**Non-skippable in-stream**: short ads that must be watched; usually bought on impressions (CPM).
**Bumper ads**: up to 6 seconds, non-skippable, bought on CPM. Good for one simple message repeated often.
**In-feed and Shorts ads**: appear in search results, next to videos or between Shorts.

Because these ads are paid differently, they are judged by different numbers. **CPM** is the cost per 1,000 impressions. **View rate** is views divided by impressions. **CPV** is cost per view. **Click-through rate (CTR)** is clicks divided by impressions, and it matters most for Search.
Worked example: reading a mixed campaign report

For example, Halima runs a fabric shop in Kano with a website. In one month (figures illustrative) she spent ₦45,000 on Display remarketing and ₦75,000 on a skippable YouTube ad showing her new lace arrivals.
Display: 450 clicks. CTR = 450 / 150,000 = 0.3%.
YouTube: 20,000 impressions and 3,000 views. View rate = 3,000 / 20,000 = 15%.
YouTube: CPV = 75,000 / 3,000 = ₦25 per view.
She compares this with her Search campaign, which spent ₦80,000 for 200 clicks (₦400 per click) and produced 18 WhatsApp enquiries.

Display and YouTube bought cheap attention, but Search produced the enquiries. Halima keeps Search as the core, keeps Display only for past visitors, and judges YouTube on whether branded searches for her shop name rise over the next two months.
Remarketing: talking to people who already know you

**Remarketing** shows ads to people who have already visited a website or app, watched a YouTube video or are on a customer list the business uploads. In Google Ads these lists are called **your data segments**. Remarketing is usually cheap and well targeted, because the audience already knows the brand. It needs a website tag or a customer list, enough visitors to form a list, and a clear privacy notice on the website explaining that data is used for advertising.

Agree with the client, before launch, how each campaign will be judged. A Search campaign is judged on cost per lead or cost per sale. An awareness campaign on YouTube is judged on cheap reach and, over a few months, on signs of interest such as more people searching for the brand name, more direct visits to the website and more "I saw your video" messages on WhatsApp. If a client expects YouTube views to behave like Search leads, they will switch it off too early and blame the channel.
Performance Max is not a shortcut

Performance Max lets Google's automation decide where to show ads across all channels, steered by your conversion goals. If conversion tracking counts the wrong thing, it will optimise hard towards the wrong thing. Use it only after tracking is proven, which is covered in lesson m2-l1.

The most common mistake in Google Ads is setting a budget and bids without knowing what a customer is worth. Clients say "spend as little as possible", but the real question is: **how much can we pay for a click and still make money?** This lesson gives you the chain of calculations that answers it. You will use it in every discovery call, every proposal and every monthly review.
A target with people around it representing a chosen audience
Knowing what one customer is worth tells you how hard you can bid to reach them.
The chain from job value to maximum CPC
**Average sale value**: what one customer pays on average.
**Gross profit per sale**: sale value multiplied by the gross margin (after direct costs such as materials and labour).
**Close rate**: out of every 10 leads (calls, forms, WhatsApp chats), how many become paying customers.
**Lead value**: gross profit per sale multiplied by the close rate.
**Target cost per lead (target CPA)**: the share of lead value the business is willing to spend on advertising.
**Maximum CPC**: target CPA multiplied by the landing page conversion rate (the share of clicks that become leads).

Worked example: a solar installer in Ibadan
For example, Tunde installs home solar systems in Ibadan. All naira figures below are illustrative and must be replaced with your client's own numbers.
Average job value is about ₦1,200,000. His gross margin is 25%, so gross profit per job = 1,200,000 x 0.25 = ₦300,000.

Tunde can afford up to about ₦500 per click. If Keyword Planner shows most of his keywords well below that, the market is workable. If they are mostly above it, he must improve his conversion rate or close rate before spending heavily.

Ask for the close rate early

Many small businesses do not know their close rate. Ask them to count, for two weeks, how many enquiries came in and how many paid. Even a rough figure from a notebook is better than a guess, and it often shows that faster replies on WhatsApp would raise lead value more than any change to the ads.
Budgets are averages

Google Ads Help explains that a campaign can spend up to two times its average daily budget on a busy day, but over a month it will not charge more than 30.4 times the average daily budget. With ₦9,900 a day, one day could reach ₦19,800, and the month is capped at about ₦300,960. Tell clients this before launch so a busy day does not cause panic.

A campaign is only as good as the data it learns from. Google's bidding tools adjust bids towards whatever you tell them is a **conversion**. If tracking counts page views as leads, the system will happily buy more page views. So the first technical job is not writing ads. It is setting up the account properly and proving that the conversion count matches reality.

Tracking set up before launch is what makes every later decision trustworthy.
Creating the account the professional way
The **client creates the account** at ads.google.com with their own business Google account, and adds their own payment method. The account and its history belong to the business, not to you.
When the sign-up flow pushes a quick "Smart campaign", look for the option to **switch to Expert mode**. Expert mode gives full control of keywords, match types, bidding and reporting.
Choose the **billing country, time zone and currency** carefully. Google does not let you change the account currency later, and reports follow the time zone.
Turn on **2-Step Verification** for every Google account with access.
Access without passwords

Never ask a client for their Google password. Instead, create a free **Google Ads manager account** (often called an MCC) for yourself, then send the client a link request from it, or ask them to invite your email under Admin, then Access and security. Google Ads offers access levels including **Admin**, **Standard**, **Read only**, **Billing** and **Email only**. For day-to-day management, Standard is usually enough. Admin is needed only for tasks such as managing users and linking some accounts.

Go to Goals, then Conversions, then Summary, and create a **conversion action**. For most service businesses the useful actions are: a form submitted (measured by a visit to a thank-you page or a form event), a click on the phone number on mobile, calls from the ad's call asset, and clicks on a WhatsApp chat link. You can track with the **Google tag** placed on the website, often through Google Tag Manager, or by **importing conversions from Google Analytics 4 (GA4)** if the site already uses it.

Worked example: finding double counting before it costs money

For example, Ifeoma runs a lesson centre in Abuja. Her previous freelancer set the form conversion to count Every, triggered by the thank-you page. In March (figures illustrative) Google Ads reported 40 leads.
Ifeoma's enquiry book for March shows 22 real form enquiries from the website.

Testing shows the thank-you page fires the tag again when parents refresh it or return to it.

Choosing a bidding strategy
**Maximize clicks**: gets as many clicks as the budget allows. Useful at launch before conversions are recorded; always set a maximum CPC limit.
**Manual CPC**: you set bids per keyword. Full control, more work.
**Maximize conversions**: Smart Bidding that seeks the most conversions within budget. Needs trustworthy tracking.
**Target CPA**: aims for an average cost per conversion you set. Set it close to the CPA the account is already achieving, then adjust gradually.
**Maximize conversion value** and **Target ROAS**: for shops where conversions have money values.

Do not change bidding strategy every few days. Smart Bidding needs time and conversion data to learn, and each big change restarts part of that learning. Make one significant change at a time, write it in your change log, and give it at least a couple of weeks before judging it, unless spend is clearly going wrong. Launching is the moment most budget mistakes happen: the wrong location, a missing negative list, a broken landing page, or a conversion that fires on every page. A short, disciplined checklist and a weekly routine prevent nearly all of them. This lesson gives you both, plus the documentation habits that make your work trustworthy.

Ad policies you will meet

Google reviews every ad and landing page against its advertising policies. Ads can be **Approved**, **Approved (limited)**, or **Disapproved**. Common problems for small businesses include: **destination** issues (broken or very slow pages, pages that do not match the ad); **editorial** issues (excessive capitals, repeated punctuation such as "!!!", gimmicky symbols); **misrepresentation** (missing business details, unrealistic promises); and **restricted** categories such as financial services, healthcare and medicines, alcohol and gambling, which may need certification or verification. Financial services advertisers in some countries must complete Google's financial services verification. Always read the policy page linked from a disapproval before editing, and never try to trick the review by showing reviewers a different page.
Scam alerts and fake 'Google agents'

Clients sometimes receive calls or emails from people claiming to be from Google, asking for account access or payment to "fix" ads. Google Ads account changes and billing happen inside the account, never by sending money to a person. Teach clients to verify any request by logging in themselves at ads.google.com.

The **search terms report** (Insights and reports, then Search terms) shows the actual searches that triggered your ads, which can differ from your keywords. Review it at least weekly in the first months. Add irrelevant searches as negatives. Add strong, converting searches as new keywords in the right ad group.

For example, in Tunde's first full week his campaign spent 7 x ₦9,900 = ₦69,300 (figures illustrative). The search terms report shows several kinds of searches.
Searches containing "jobs", "vacancy" or "training" cost ₦8,400 with 0 leads. Share of spend: 8,400 / 69,300 = about 12.1%.

On Wednesday the campaign spent ₦18,500. That is under 2 x ₦9,900 = ₦19,800, so it is within normal daily variation.
About 12% of the week's spend was going to job seekers. Blocking those searches frees that money for real buyers from the next week.
Testing ads without guesswork

Ad testing is part of the weekly loop. Keep two responsive search ads in your most important ad groups, each with a different angle: for example one built around speed ("Installed This Week") and one around trust ("Certified Installers"). Let them run until each has a meaningful number of clicks before you decide. Then compare CTR and, more importantly, conversion rate. An ad with a slightly lower CTR but a higher conversion rate usually wins, because it brings the right people. Replace the loser with a new angle and record the result.

Look at the **asset details** for each RSA too. Google labels headlines and descriptions with performance ratings once there is enough data. Replace assets that stay rated Low with new wording, but keep your best claims. Small, steady improvements every few weeks add up over a quarter.

Fixes that save a lot and take an hour, such as adding negatives or correcting a conversion setting, go first. Bigger jobs, such as rebuilding the account structure or a new landing page, go into a phased plan with dates. Write each finding in the same pattern: what you saw, the number that proves it, why it matters, and the fix.

Also check the basics clients often miss: whether the account uses Search Partners or the Display Network inside a Search campaign without anyone deciding to, whether ads run at night when nobody answers the phone, whether the business phone number in the call asset is still correct, and whether the Google Business Profile is linked for location assets. Every Google Ads engagement has two different costs. **Ad spend** is paid by the client directly to Google, from their own payment method, for clicks and impressions. Your **management fee** pays for your time and skill. Mixing these up causes most pricing arguments. Say it plainly in every conversation and in writing: "Your ad budget goes to Google. My fee is for managing it."

Common fee models

Many freelancers use a flat fee with a setup charge, and agree in writing when it will be reviewed.

A third option is a **hybrid**: a one-off setup fee for discovery, tracking and build, then a monthly management fee. Some managers add a minimum fee plus a percentage above a spend level. Avoid fees tied only to leads or sales unless you control the landing page and the client's follow-up, because outcomes depend on both.
Pricing from your hours

Price from the work, not from a figure you heard online. List the tasks for setup and for a typical month, estimate hours honestly, and multiply by your hourly rate. Research current rates in your market and level by asking peers and checking freelance platforms, and adjust as your results grow.
Worked example: pricing an account for a Lagos events company
For example, Amaka is pricing Google Ads management for an events company that plans a ₦600,000 monthly ad budget. Her working rate is ₦12,000 per hour. All amounts are illustrative.
Setup: discovery 2 hours, tracking 4, keyword research 3, campaign build and ads 5, QA 2. Total 16 hours x ₦12,000 = ₦192,000; she quotes a setup fee of ₦200,000.
Monthly work: weekly search terms and optimisation 4 x 1.5 = 6 hours, ad testing 2, report and call 2. Total 10 hours x ₦12,000 = ₦120,000 per month.
Percentage check: 15% of ₦600,000 = ₦90,000, which would not cover her 10 hours.
If the budget later rises to ₦1,200,000, 15% would be ₦180,000, but her hours might only rise to 12 (₦144,000).
She offers: ₦200,000 setup, then ₦120,000 a month, reviewed after 3 months or if ad spend changes by more than half.

The client's first-month cost is ₦600,000 to Google plus ₦320,000 to Amaka (setup and month one). From month two it is ₦600,000 plus ₦120,000. The fee matches the work, and the review clause keeps it fair.
What the proposal must say
**Goal and measure**: for example, qualified enquiries tracked by form, call and WhatsApp, checked against the client's own log.
**Included**: campaigns and networks covered, number of ad groups at launch, weekly optimisation, one monthly report and call.
**Not included**: landing page design, website fixes, video production, extra campaigns, daily on-demand changes. Price these separately.
**Client duties**: own the account and payment method, approve ad claims, answer leads promptly, share sales feedback monthly.
**Timeline**: setup in a set number of working days, a learning period, first review at 30 days.
**Payment and exit**: fee paid in advance by bank transfer or a payment link (for example Paystack), notice period, and access handover on exit.
Controlling scope after you start

Scope creep is the slow growth of work without a change in price. It often starts kindly: "Can you also boost this Instagram post?" or "Please check our website copy." Each request is small, but together they can double your hours. Agree a simple rule in the proposal: requests outside the listed scope get a short written quote before you start. Keep a running list of these requests and their hours, and bring it to the monthly call so the client sees the extra work.

Set a **response time** too. For example, messages answered within one working day, urgent issues such as disapproved ads or a broken landing page handled the same day. Say which channel is for what: WhatsApp for quick questions, email for approvals of ad claims and budget changes, because email leaves a clearer record. If the client wants daily changes or weekend cover, that is a higher service level with a higher fee.

Finally, protect cash flow. Ask for the setup fee before you begin, and monthly fees in advance at the start of each month. Issue a simple invoice each time with your business name, the period covered and the services, and keep copies for your records and tax.

Never guarantee positions, a number of leads or a cost per lead before the account has data. A small budget gives small results however skilled you are. Say what the first 30 days are for: proving tracking, finding the keywords that convert and cutting waste.

Most adverts interrupt people. A search ad shows only after someone has typed what they want into Google.
When a person in Ibadan types inverter installation near me, she is telling you her need, her place and often her hurry. That is called search intent.
Every search runs a fresh auction among advertisers whose keywords match. Nobody books a fixed spot.
The winner is not simply the person who bids most. Quality counts too, and quality is something you control.
The most common mistake in Google Ads is setting a budget and bids without knowing what a customer is worth. This video shows you how to work it out.
Quality Score
The three parts of Quality Score
How likely your ad is to be clicked. Put the searcher's words and a clear offer in the headline.
How closely the ad matches the search. Split keywords into tight themes, one need per ad.
How useful the page is after the click. Send people to the matching page, fast on mobile.
Google gives each keyword a Quality Score from 1 to 10. Think of it as a warning light. It has three parts.
First, expected click-through rate, or CTR: how likely your ad is to be clicked.
Second, ad relevance. If this is low, the keyword probably sits in the wrong ad group.
Third, landing page experience. If this is below average, cleverer ads will not fix it. Fix the page.
In the course example, Installer A bids 300 naira with good quality, takes the top spot and pays about 251 naira a click, while Installer B bids 500 naira and sits lower.
Step by step
From job value to maximum CPC
Close rate: how many leads pay
Lead value = profit x close rate
Maximum CPC = target x conversion rate
Know what a customer is worth before you set any bid.
Here is the chain you will use in every proposal. Start with the average sale value.
Next, gross profit per sale: the sale value times the gross margin, after materials and labour.
Then the close rate. Out of every 10 leads, how many pay?
Multiply gross profit by the close rate, and you have the lead value.
Decide what share of lead value the business will spend on ads. That is the target cost per lead.
Multiply that by the landing page conversion rate, the share of clicks that become leads. That is your maximum CPC, the most you can pay for a click and still make money.

Discovery call
Six areas to ask about
Economics: sale value and margin
Sales: how many of 10 enquiries pay?
Customer: what do they type, from where?
Offer: why choose you over the next ad?
History: what was tried and what it cost
Capacity: how many new jobs a month?
On the discovery call, first ask what an average sale is worth and the margin they keep. Then ask how many of 10 enquiries pay, and who answers calls and WhatsApp, and how fast.
Ask what customers type when looking for them, and where they come from. And ask why someone should choose them over the next three ads.
Ask what advertising they tried and what happened. Finally, ask about capacity. If a caterer can only do four events a month and three are booked, a big campaign creates angry customers, not profit.
Audit order
Audit an account in this order
Fix measurement first. Every other number rests on it.
Ask for Read only access through your manager account, then audit in a fixed order. First, tracking. Do reported conversions match the client's own records?
Second, search terms. What share of spend went to irrelevant searches in the last 30 days?
Third, structure. Look for huge ad groups, or broad match running without reliable tracking.
Fourth, ads and pages. Do ads match their ad groups? Are pages slow on mobile?
Fifth, budget and bidding.

For example, Chika's furniture account reported a cost per conversion of about 2,143 naira. But it counted visits to the Contact page. Against her own log, each real lead cost about 12,857 naira. So fix measurement first.

Does not reward overspending
Review it if work grows
Percentage of spend
Grows with account size
Can look like a push to spend
Remember there are two costs. Ad spend goes from the client to Google. Your management fee pays for your time and skill.
A flat monthly fee is easy to budget for and does not reward overspending, but review it if the work grows.
A percentage of spend grows with the account, but small budgets give tiny fees, and it can look like a reason to spend more. Many freelancers use a setup fee plus a flat monthly fee.

Money rules for every client
Say it plainly: your ad budget goes to Google. My fee is for managing it.
Setup fee before you begin, monthly fees at the start of each month, with an invoice each time.

Three money rules protect you both. First, keep spend and fee separate, and say so in writing.

Third, never guarantee positions, leads or a cost per lead before the account has data. The first 30 days are for proving tracking, finding keywords that convert and cutting waste.
